summary: North Macedonia grants 90 visa-free days to citizens of the EU, UK, US, most of the Americas and its Balkan neighbors, while visa-required nationalities can either apply at an embassy or enter for up to 15 days per visit on a valid multiple-entry Schengen visa, an EU residence permit or (through 2026) a multiple-entry US, UK or Canadian visa.

defaultStayWindow.text: A short stay, with or without a visa, may last no longer than 90 days in any 180-day period, counted back from each day of the stay. A foreigner who needs no visa must leave by the end of those 90 days.

source.name: Law on Foreigners, consolidated text — published by the Ministry of Internal Affairs
source.instrument: Law on Foreigners (Official Gazette 97/2018, as amended), Art. 2(9) (short stay: no longer than 90 days in any 180-day period preceding each day of stay), Art. 11(1) and Art. 21 (a foreigner who needs no visa leaves by the end of 90 days in the 180 preceding each day of stay)

conditionalWaivers.text: Holders of a valid multiple-entry US, UK or Canadian visa in their passport, valid at least five days beyond the planned stay, may enter North Macedonia without a visa for up to 15 days, under a temporary government decision in force from 1 January to 31 December 2026. Holders of a valid multiple-entry Schengen (type C) visa valid at least five days beyond the stay, and third-country nationals with temporary or permanent residence in an EU or Schengen state, may also stay up to 15 days per entry, within 90 days in any 180-day period.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published. Under the Law on Foreigners, every foreigner entering for a short stay must justify the purpose and conditions of the stay and have means of subsistence for it and for the return or onward journey; the Government sets the amount by decision, but no figure is published. Means can be shown with cash, traveller's cheques or credit cards, and short-stay (C) visa applicants must prove them with their application, for example with a credit card or bank statement.

declarations.name: Registration of foreigners
declarations.text: You must register with the local police in the town or city where you are staying within 48 hours of arrival. Hotel staff register you at check-in; otherwise register with the police directly (also possible online, in Macedonian) and de-register 24 hours before you leave. Keep the registration document until you leave: failing to register can bring a fine, detention and a court hearing, or a restriction on returning.

currencyLimits.text: Non-residents must declare foreign cash and cheques worth €10,000 or more on entry; smaller sums can be declared voluntarily. On departure a non-resident may not take out more foreign cash than was declared on entry.

payments.text: Canada's travel advice says North Macedonia's economy is mostly cash-based, with credit cards accepted in some larger establishments and ATMs in urban centres; Australia's Smartraveller says major hotels and large shops accept cards. The UK government advises changing money only at banks or official exchanges, and the denar cannot be exchanged outside the country.

safety.text: The UK government says attacks against foreign nationals are extremely rare, but gangs of children pickpocket and bag-snatch in the main shopping and entertainment areas late at night, and there are occasional shooting incidents, including in Skopje, not targeted at foreign nationals. Canada says secondary roads are poorly maintained and lack adequate lighting.

tips.text: Register with the police soon after you arrive: Canada says within 24 hours, the UK government within 48 hours. Hotels and other commercial accommodation register you at check-in; otherwise register at the nearest police station and keep the document until you leave.

Canada says the economy is mostly cash-based and cards are accepted only in some larger establishments. The UK government says to change money only through banks or official exchanges, not through street dealers.

Canada's travel advice says smoke haze and air pollution can be extremely hazardous, usually worst in winter because of coal and wood heating, and Australia's Smartraveller names Skopje. It advises talking to your doctor before you travel if you have a breathing condition.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for North Macedonia?
faq.answer: Most Western travelers don't: citizens of the EU, UK, US, Canada, Australia, Japan and most of the Americas can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period visa-free. Nationalities that need a visa can apply at a North Macedonian embassy, or enter for up to 15 days per visit if they hold a valid multiple-entry Schengen visa or EU residence permit, or, under a decision in force through 31 December 2026, a valid multiple-entry US, UK or Canadian visa.

faq.question: Can I enter North Macedonia with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Yes — holders of a valid multiple-entry Schengen (type C) visa can enter without a North Macedonian visa and stay up to 15 days per visit, provided the Schengen visa remains valid at least five days beyond the stay.

faq.question: How long can US citizens stay in North Macedonia?
faq.answer: US passport holders can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period without a visa.

faq.question: What currency is used in North Macedonia?
faq.answer: The Macedonian denar (MKD). Canada's travel advice says the economy is mostly cash-based, with credit cards accepted in some larger establishments and ATMs in urban centres. Australia's Smartraveller says the denar cannot be changed outside North Macedonia.

faq.question: Can EU citizens enter North Macedonia with just an ID card?
faq.answer: Yes. The Foreign Ministry says nationals of EU member states and Schengen signatories do not need a visa and may enter with a valid national identity card.
